findings.requirement_type: Primary CGL — Coverage Scope vs. Election Services Operations
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance ... The policy shall include coverage for premises liability, bodily injury, broad form property damage, personal injury, products and completed operations and blanket contractual coverage, and shall not contain any provisions which would serve to limit third party action over claims.
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County contract / Sacramento County Appendix G
findings.policy_quote: This insurance applies only to the insured's operations for which a classification is listed on the declaration page of this policy. If any classification is not shown, the corresponding insured's operations is not insured hereunder.
findings.gap_description: The CGL provided in the package is the Arch 'Liability Policy – Security Guards' monoline, restricted by Classification Limitation Endorsement 00 GL0713 to NCCI codes 91127 (alarms), 91636 (detective/investigative), and 98751 (security & patrol agencies). Run-Test Election Services' core operations — ballot printing, election mail processing, election technology — are NOT covered by this policy. The umbrella's Schedule of Underlying Policies (Pg 14) references a separate Citizens CGL (ZB4 H221415 05) at $1M/$2M which is presumably the primary GL responding to election operations, but that policy was not included in this analysis package and cannot be audited.
findings.plain_english: The general liability policy in your file only covers your in-house security guard operations. It does not cover the actual business that your county contracts are about — printing ballots, processing election mail, handling voter data. Your real primary GL (the Citizens policy listed in the umbrella schedule) was not provided for review, so we cannot confirm that it meets either Sacramento's or Maricopa's contract requirements. This is the most important policy in the program for these contracts and we are flying blind on it.
findings.recommendation: Immediately obtain and audit the Citizens CGL (ZB4 H221415 05) listed on the umbrella's Schedule of Underlying Policies, including the dec page, all endorsements, and the AI/WoS/P&NC forms. Confirm classification matches election services operations (ballot printing, mail processing, election technology). Until the primary CGL is reviewed, county compliance cannot be certified.
discoveryQuestions: Has Sacramento or Maricopa ever asked to see the actual policy and endorsement copies — not just the COI — and which policy did your broker send them?

When you signed the Maricopa and Sacramento contracts, who at your broker confirmed your election-services operations were covered under the right CGL classification — not just the security-guard policy?
If a voter or county claimed that a misprocessed ballot caused them harm, do you know with certainty which GL policy your carrier would point to?
Have you ever had a coverage attorney or risk consultant cross-check that your operations classifications on your CGL match what you actually do day-to-day?

findings.requirement_type: Minimum Limits — General Liability ($2M/$4M Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance ... with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Each Occurrence Limit: $1,000,000 / General Aggregate Limit: $3,000,000 / Products-Completed Operations Aggregate: $3,000,000
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $2M occurrence / $4M general aggregate / $4M products-completed ops aggregate. The Security Guards CGL provides $1M / $3M / $3M. The Citizens primary CGL (per umbrella schedule) is also $1M occurrence / $2M general aggregate — also below Maricopa minimums on a stand-alone basis. Maricopa §8.2.9 + §8.2.10 explicitly permit umbrella stacking on CGL — the $10M Hanover umbrella, if confirmed to follow form over the Citizens primary CGL, would cure the limit gap.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $2M per claim and $4M total per year on general liability. None of your underlying GL policies hit that on their own — but Maricopa's contract specifically allows you to use your $10M umbrella to bridge the gap. As long as the umbrella sits properly over the right primary CGL, you are compliant. The risk is if the umbrella interpretation breaks down or doesn't follow form on a specific claim type.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Hanover that the $10M umbrella follows form over the Citizens primary CGL for Maricopa-related operations. Issue a COI to Maricopa explicitly indicating umbrella stacking on the CGL line per §8.2.9. For long-term, consider increasing primary CGL to $2M to remove dependency on umbrella stacking and simplify compliance with future county contracts that may not permit umbrella to count.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Umbrella ($10M) — assuming follow-form over the Citizens primary CGL
discoveryQuestions: Does the certificate of insurance you provided to Maricopa County clearly indicate that the umbrella sits over the GL — not just list the umbrella separately?
If you won a contract tomorrow with a county that didn't allow umbrella stacking, would you know what your true primary GL limit needs to be?
Have you considered that as the contract count grows from 31 states, more counties will start requiring $2M primary instead of $1M — and what increasing the primary limit would cost?

findings.requirement_type: Missing Cyber Liability Policy
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to ... regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity ...
findings.policy_quote: [No standalone cyber policy provided in this audit package. CGL contains absolute exclusions: CG 21 06 (Access/Disclosure of Confidential Material), CG 00 69 (Violation of Law Addressing Data Privacy — explicitly names BIPA, CCPA, GDPR), and CG 40 35 (Cyber Incident). Hanover Umbrella contains 475-0654, 475-0655, and 475-0661 absolute cyber/privacy exclusions on BOTH Coverage A and Coverage B.]
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $5M Cyber, Network Security & Privacy Liability covering data breach, regulatory defense plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, business interruption, computer fraud, funds transfer, and third-party fidelity. No cyber policy was included in the audit package. The CGL has triple-stacked cyber exclusions (data privacy, personal info disclosure, cyber incident) that strip every category of cyber loss from GL. The umbrella has matching exclusions on both Coverage A and Coverage B — so even if a primary cyber policy existed and were exhausted, the umbrella would not drop down. For an election services vendor handling voter PII for 90M+ registered voters across 31 states, a cyber breach is the single largest financial and reputational exposure.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa County requires you to carry $5M in cyber insurance with very specific coverages — data breach response, regulatory fines, ransomware, business interruption, funds transfer fraud, and third-party theft. We did not see a cyber policy in your package. Your GL policy specifically excludes every flavor of cyber claim, and your umbrella does too. If you had a ransomware attack, a voter data breach, a wire fraud loss, or a regulatory inquiry under CCPA or a state election law, NONE of your current insurance would respond. Given that election infrastructure is a top-tier target for nation-state actors and you handle personal data for 90 million voters, this is the most existential gap in your program.
findings.recommendation: If a standalone Cyber policy is not in force, place one IMMEDIATELY at $5M minimum to satisfy Maricopa §8.2.13 and to address the underlying exposure. The form must include, at minimum: third-party privacy/network security liability, regulatory defense AND fines/penalties, cyber extortion (with sublimit increase for ransomware), business interruption AND dependent BI, computer fraud, social engineering / funds transfer fraud (full limit, not sublimited), data restoration, and breach response. Specifically test the form against each enumerated coverage in §8.2.13. If a cyber policy IS in force but was simply not provided, produce it for full audit. Note: third-party fidelity and computer fraud may also require attention on a Crime/Fidelity policy.
discoveryQuestions: When was the last time you simulated a ransomware attack on your ballot processing systems — and do you know who would pay for the forensic, restoration, and notification costs?
If a state attorney general opened an investigation into how you handle voter data under their state's privacy law, would your insurance pay for the lawyers and any fines, or only the lawyers?
You handle personal data for 90M+ voters across 31 states — has anyone walked you through what your largest single claim could look like under CCPA, BIPA, or an election-law privacy statute?

Maricopa specifically requires third-party fidelity coverage as part of cyber — has anyone confirmed that your cyber form (or crime form) actually includes that, or is it sublimited to a meaningless number?

findings.requirement_type: Missing Professional Liability / Technology E&O Policy
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... UMBRELLA or Excess Liability ... shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements where necessary for Commercial General Liability, Commercial Automobile Liability, Employers' Liability, and any other liability coverage (other than Professional Liability) designated under the Minimum Scope of Insurance.
findings.policy_quote: Coverage A — This insurance does not apply to any liability arising out of: (1) the rendering of or failure to render any 'professional services'; ... (Hanover Umbrella, 475-0031). Section VII.3.k. Coverage B — This insurance does not apply to: ... 'bodily injury,' 'property damage,' 'personal injury' or 'advertising injury' arising out of the rendering or failure to render any 'professional services' ...
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires $1M/$1M Professional Liability and explicitly states umbrella CANNOT be used to satisfy this minimum. No standalone Professional Liability / Technology E&O policy was included in the audit package. The CGL Coverage D 'E&O Coverage Extension' (00 GL1049, Pg 23) exists but is (a) limited to security operations classifications only, (b) shares the General Aggregate and Each Occurrence limits with A/B/C (not separate aggregate), (c) excludes contractual liability except insured contracts, and (d) is therefore not a substitute for genuine Professional Liability. The umbrella expressly excludes Professional Liability on both Coverage A and B. For an election services vendor providing 'cutting-edge technology' for ballot printing, election mail sorting, and emergency support — a single misprocessed ballot batch, a software defect in election technology, or a missed mailing could generate claims well into the seven figures and there would be NO coverage anywhere in the program.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County requires you to carry $1M of Professional Liability / Errors & Omissions coverage and explicitly forbids using your umbrella to meet this requirement. We did not see a Professional Liability / Tech E&O policy in your package. Your election technology, ballot processing, and mail handling are the textbook definition of 'professional services' — and a mistake (a software bug, a printing error, a delayed mailing) could cost a county its election. Without a real E&O policy, you are out of contract compliance with Sacramento AND uninsured for the most likely large-loss scenario you face: a screw-up in your core service. Your GL has a small E&O extension but it (i) only covers security ops, (ii) shares limits with general liability, and (iii) is not a substitute. Your umbrella expressly excludes Professional Liability.
findings.recommendation: If a standalone Professional / Tech E&O policy is not in force, place one IMMEDIATELY at $1M/$1M minimum (consider $5M+ for the actual exposure). Definition of 'Professional Services' must explicitly cover: ballot printing, election mail processing/sorting, election technology hardware and software, voter data processing, emergency election support, and consultative services to election officials. Confirm retro date on or before the earliest county contract effective date (Sacramento §V.A) and confirm at least 1-year ERP/tail (Sacramento §V.C) and 2-year ERP for Maricopa §8.2.3. If an E&O is in force but not provided, produce it for audit.
discoveryQuestions: If a misprinted ballot or a delayed mail drop forced a county to delay or rerun its election, what do you think the county's damages would look like — and do you have a policy that responds?
Sacramento explicitly says you cannot use your umbrella to satisfy their E&O requirement — were you aware of that, and how did your broker certify compliance to them?

Your services include cutting-edge election technology and software — when was the last time the definition of 'professional services' on your E&O was tested against a real-world ballot processing claim scenario?
If a federal claim came in tomorrow alleging your ballot scanner software was responsible for an election-day miscount, do you know what limit, retro date, and exclusions you'd be relying on?

findings.requirement_type: Missing Crime / Fidelity Policy
findings.contract_quote: Cyber ... shall include ... computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: [No Crime/Fidelity policy provided. GL contains Limited Theft Extension Endorsement 00 GL1045 with $100,000 per occurrence / $300,000 aggregate sublimits, but excludes theft by insured/employees, money/securities in transit, and inventory shortages — therefore not employee dishonesty / fidelity coverage.]
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's cyber requirement explicitly mandates third-party fidelity, computer fraud, and funds transfer loss. While these can be written within a cyber form, market practice for higher-quality coverage is a separate Crime policy. No Crime/Fidelity policy is in the audit package. For a PE-backed manufacturer with 50–200 employees handling election mail and large customer payments, employee theft and social engineering / wire fraud are realistic exposures. If the cyber policy (when produced) does not include adequate third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer, and social engineering with non-sublimited limits, a separate Crime policy is required to cure both the contract gap and the underlying exposure.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants you to carry coverage for: (1) employee theft of client property, (2) computer fraud, and (3) wire transfer / funds transfer fraud. We did not see a Crime / Fidelity policy in your package. These can sometimes be packaged into Cyber, but only with the right form. If your cyber policy sublimits social engineering to $100k or excludes employee theft of client funds, you are uninsured. For an election services company moving large invoices and handling counties' funds and ballot mail, this is a real risk.
findings.recommendation: Verify that the Cyber policy (when produced) includes third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer, and social engineering coverage with limits that meet Maricopa's $5M expectation — NOT sublimits. If gaps remain, place a separate Crime policy with: Employee Theft (Including Clients' Property), Forgery or Alteration, Inside/Outside the Premises, Computer & Funds Transfer Fraud, Social Engineering Fraud, and Client Property coverage at minimum $1M–$5M depending on cash/transaction exposure.
discoveryQuestions: If an employee in your accounting team was tricked by a wire-fraud email into sending $250,000 to a fake vendor, where would that loss land — your cyber policy, your crime policy, or your balance sheet?
Do you know whether the cyber policy you may have actually covers employee theft of client property — Maricopa specifically requires 'third-party fidelity' as part of cyber?
When was the last time you had an outside auditor stress-test your fraud controls and confirm that your insurance would respond if they failed?

findings.requirement_type: Auto Liability Policy — Not Included in Audit Package
findings.contract_quote: Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit. (Sacramento). Commercial/Business Automobile Liability ... not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence ... owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles. (Maricopa)
findings.policy_quote: [Auto Schedule of Underlying — Allmerica AW4 H221414 05 — $1M each accident — listed in Hanover Umbrella Schedule of Underlying, Pg 14. Underlying Auto policy itself NOT included in audit package.]
findings.gap_description: An Allmerica Commercial Auto policy (AW4 H221414 05, $1M CSL) is referenced in the umbrella's Schedule of Underlying Policies but the Auto policy itself was not provided for audit. Cannot evaluate: (a) Symbol assignment (1 vs 7 vs 8/9), (b) Hired/Non-Owned coverage, (c) Drive Other Car, (d) Fellow Employee deletion, (e) MCS-90 if applicable, (f) UM/UIM, (g) Auto AI / WoS / P&NC endorsements, (h) Lease Gap / Mobile Equipment definitions. Sacramento requires $1M CSL — Auto stand-alone of $1M would meet. Maricopa requires $2M CSL — Auto stand-alone of $1M does NOT meet on its own; Maricopa §8.2.9 program-level umbrella permission combined with §8.2.11 Auto clause that does NOT inline-mention umbrella creates an interpretive ambiguity (see finding-007).
findings.plain_english: We could not audit your Auto policy because it wasn't provided. We can see it exists from the umbrella schedule, but we cannot tell you whether the symbols are right, whether hired/non-owned coverage is included, whether the additional insured form is broad enough for the counties, or whether your fellow-employee exclusion has been deleted. The Auto policy is the second-most-likely thing to generate a county claim (election supplies in transit, employee driving to a polling site) so flying blind on it is not acceptable. Please get it audited.
findings.recommendation: Obtain and audit the Allmerica Auto policy. Specifically verify: Symbol 1 'any auto' assignment for liability, Hired & Non-Owned coverage included, blanket AI by contract endorsement, blanket Waiver of Subrogation, Primary & Noncontributory, Fellow Employee Exclusion deletion, Notice & Knowledge officer-limited endorsement, Drive Other Car if owners take vehicles home, UM/UIM compliance per AZ requirements.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Auto Limit — Umbrella Attachment Ambiguous
findings.contract_quote: §8.2.9: If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements. ... §8.2.11: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit ... not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence ...
findings.policy_quote: Underlying Auto — Allmerica AW4 H221414 05 — $1M each accident (Hanover Schedule of Underlying, Pg 14). Hanover Umbrella $10M limit (Pg 24).
findings.gap_description: Strict reading: §8.2.11 Auto sets a $2M CSL minimum and does not inline-mention umbrella stacking. Under that reading, $1M Auto + $10M Umbrella does NOT cure the $2M Auto minimum because the umbrella stacking is not authorized at the Auto line. Permissive reading: §8.2.9 grants program-level umbrella permission for any line. Under that reading, $1M + $10M = $11M, well in excess. Maricopa's risk manager has not been asked which reading they apply. The $1M Auto stand-alone is below the $2M Maricopa minimum, so the question matters.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract has two clauses that could be read together — one says you can use umbrella to meet limits in general, the other lists a $2M auto requirement without mentioning umbrella. Depending on which way you read them, your $1M auto + $10M umbrella either complies easily or doesn't comply at all. We need to ask Maricopa's risk manager directly which reading they enforce. Don't assume.
findings.recommendation: Email Maricopa County Risk Management (301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910) before the next renewal cycle requesting written confirmation that umbrella stacking applies to the Auto line. If Maricopa rejects the permissive reading, increase primary Auto CSL to $2M.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Umbrella ($10M) — IF permissive reading applies

findings.requirement_type: Workers' Compensation Policy — Not Included in Audit Package + California Other-States Coverage
findings.contract_quote: WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance. ... EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident for bodily injury or disease. (Sacramento). Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes ... Employer's Liability $1,000,000/$1,000,000/$1,000,000. (Maricopa)
findings.policy_quote: [WC Schedule of Underlying — Mass Bay WD4 H218283 06 — $1M/$1M/$1M EL — listed in Hanover Umbrella Schedule of Underlying, Pg 14. Underlying WC policy itself NOT included in audit package.]
findings.gap_description: A Mass Bay WC policy (WD4 H218283 06, $1M/$1M/$1M EL) is referenced in the umbrella schedule but not included in this audit. Run-Test is AZ-based but performs work for Sacramento County in California. California is NCCI-non-compliant — California WC must be statutory California or extended via a properly drafted Other States Coverage endorsement. Cannot verify: (a) AZ as Item 3.A primary state, (b) California as 3.A or via 3.C Other States with proper extension language, (c) Item 3.A states for the other 30 states Run-Test serves, (d) Waiver of Subrogation by state (CA WC 04 03 06; AZ blanket WoS form), (e) Alternate Employer endorsement if leased workers used, (f) Owners' coverage / inclusion-exclusion elections, (g) experience modification factor and trend.
findings.plain_english: Your workers' comp policy was not provided. You operate in 31 states and you take work from California — which is the toughest WC state in the country. We cannot tell you whether you have proper California coverage, whether all 31 states are listed correctly, whether the waiver of subrogation forms specific to each state are in place, or what your experience mod is doing year over year. You need to get the WC audited before performing any more California work or you risk serious uninsured exposure.
findings.recommendation: Obtain Mass Bay WC policy. Verify Item 3.A includes AZ + every state Run-Test has employees in. Verify Item 3.C Other States includes any state where work could spill over. For California specifically — confirm CA is on Item 3.A (preferred) or that Other States Coverage is robust. Confirm WC Waiver of Subrogation endorsement is in place for both AZ (general WoS) and CA (WC 04 03 06 form). Pull the experience mod history and review the loss runs. If staffing or PEO is used, confirm Alternate Employer endorsement (Sacramento §VIII; Maricopa §8.2.12).

findings.requirement_type: Missing EPLI / Employment Practices Liability
findings.contract_quote: [Not directly mandated by Sacramento or Maricopa, but employment-related claims fall outside CGL coverage.]
findings.policy_quote: This insurance does not apply to: 'Bodily injury' or 'personal and advertising injury' to: a. A person arising out of any: (1) Refusal to employ that person; (2) Termination of that person's employment; or (3) Employment-related practices, policies, acts or omissions ... including coercion, demotion, evaluation, reassignment, discipline, defamation, harassment, humiliation, discrimination ... (CGL CG 21 47). Hanover Umbrella 475-0215 excludes Discrimination on both Coverage A and B.
findings.gap_description: CGL includes the standard ISO Employment-Related Practices Exclusion (CG 21 47), and the umbrella has an absolute Discrimination Exclusion (475-0215). No standalone EPLI policy was included in the audit package. Run-Test has 50–200 employees across 31 states (high-EPLI-exposure spread including CA). Employment-related claims (wrongful termination, harassment, discrimination, retaliation, wage/hour) are uninsured anywhere in this program if no EPLI is in force.
findings.plain_english: Your GL excludes employment-related claims, and your umbrella excludes discrimination. We did not see a separate Employment Practices Liability policy in the file. With 50–200 employees in 31 states, including California — which is the most plaintiff-friendly employment-law state in the country — this is a real exposure. One harassment or wrongful-termination suit can cost six figures in defense costs alone, even if dismissed.
findings.recommendation: If EPLI is not in force, place a standalone EPLI policy at $1M minimum (consider $2M+ given multi-state and CA exposure). Form should include: Third-party coverage (harassment by non-employees / customers / vendors), Wage & Hour defense costs sublimit (CA exposure mandatory), broad definition of Employee covering temporary and contract workers, no Hammer Clause or low Hammer ratio. If EPLI is in force but not provided, produce for audit.
discoveryQuestions: You have 50–200 employees and operate in California — has your HR team had any EEOC charges, formal complaints, or termination disputes in the last 24 months that you were nervous about?
If a former employee filed a wrongful-termination suit tomorrow, do you know what policy would defend you and what would happen with the legal bills?
California has wage-and-hour class action exposure that's specific to that state — does your EPLI (if you have one) include defense for those claims, or is it sublimited?

findings.requirement_type: Named Insured Asymmetry — Inc vs LLC Across Program
findings.contract_quote: [Not contract-driven — program-level coherence finding.]
findings.policy_quote: CGL — Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services LLC'. Form of Business: Limited Liability Company. (CGL Pg 7, FAIC-SKLBUS-CPD). Hanover Umbrella — Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services Inc' (Pg 24, Dec). Multiple Named Insured Endorsement 475-0174 (Pg 56) adds Runbeck Properties LLC, Runbeck Investments LLC, Runbeck Graphics Inc.
findings.gap_description: The CGL Dec lists Named Insured as 'Runbeck Election Services LLC' and Form of Business as Limited Liability Company. The Umbrella Dec lists Named Insured as 'Runbeck Election Services Inc' (a corporation). These are two different legal entities. If Runbeck Election Services is in fact an LLC (as the CGL indicates) then the Umbrella does not properly cover the operating entity — the umbrella names a non-existent or different entity. The Umbrella Multiple Named Insured Endorsement 475-0174 explicitly schedules the affiliates (Properties LLC, Investments LLC, Graphics Inc) but does NOT include any LLC version of the Election Services entity. Conversely, if the proper legal name IS 'Runbeck Election Services Inc' (corporation), then the CGL Dec is wrong. Either way, there is a legal-entity mismatch that could be raised by a carrier as a basis for denial when a claim hits.
findings.plain_english: Your general liability policy names you as 'Runbeck Election Services LLC' and lists you as a Limited Liability Company. Your umbrella names you as 'Runbeck Election Services Inc' — a corporation. Those are two different legal entities. If a county sues 'Runbeck Election Services LLC' and the umbrella is needed, the umbrella carrier could argue it doesn't cover that entity because the umbrella names 'Inc.' This is the kind of paperwork problem that nobody notices until there's a claim — and then it becomes a million-dollar question.
findings.recommendation: Immediately verify the correct legal entity name and structure (LLC vs. Inc) by pulling the AZ Corporation Commission filing. Then issue an endorsement on whichever policy is wrong to align the Named Insured. If the entity is actually an LLC, the Umbrella needs 475-0174 amended to add the LLC. If the entity is actually an Inc, the CGL Dec needs correction. Also confirm contract counterparties (Sacramento, Maricopa) are contracting with the correct legal entity name on the SOW/Master Agreement.
discoveryQuestions: What is the actual legal name of the entity that signed the Maricopa and Sacramento contracts — and have you compared it to the named insured on every policy?
Did Runbeck Election Services convert from a corporation to an LLC (or vice versa) at any point — and was every insurance policy reissued after that change?

If you got a lawsuit served tomorrow naming 'Runbeck Election Services LLC' and your umbrella names 'Runbeck Election Services Inc', who at your broker is responsible for explaining that to the carrier?

findings.requirement_type: CGL Additional Insured — Blanket Ongoing & Completed Operations
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.A — additional insureds as respects: liability arising out of activities ... products and completed operations ... no endorsed limitations on the scope of protection. Maricopa §8.2.7 — additional insureds.
findings.policy_quote: CG 20 10 12 19 (Pg 60) — Schedule: 'ALL PARTIES WHERE REQUIRED BY A WRITTEN CONTRACT PROVIDED SUCH CONTRACT WAS EXECUTED PRIOR TO LOSS.' Companion CG 20 37 12 19 (Pg 62) provides AI for completed operations on the same blanket basis.
findings.gap_description: CGL has both ongoing operations (CG 20 10 12 19) and completed operations (CG 20 37 12 19) blanket-by-contract Additional Insured endorsements. Combined, this satisfies the 'ongoing AND completed operations' requirement on Sacramento §VII.A and the AI requirement on Maricopa §8.2.7. NOTE: AI status only applies to security operations under this monoline — real compliance depends on the same forms appearing on the primary CGL responding to election services. Trigger condition is contract executed PRIOR to loss (best practice — should be PRIOR to work in some markets but this form is acceptable). Limitation: AI coverage capped at lesser of contract-required limit or policy limit.
findings.plain_english: Your security-guards GL has both the ongoing-operations and completed-operations additional insured forms — and they're both blanket by contract. That's the right setup for the county requirements. The catch is this only covers your security-guard operations. The same forms need to be on your real primary GL (the Citizens policy) for actual contract compliance.
findings.recommendation: Confirm CG 20 10 + CG 20 37 (or equivalents) are also on the Citizens primary CGL. Consider asking carriers for the latest CG 20 10 04 13 / CG 20 37 04 13 edition vs. the 12 19 edition (different scope of 'caused in whole or in part' language). For Sacramento, note that CG 20 10/37 includes 'not broader than required by contract' language — Sacramento §VII.A says 'no endorsed limitations on the scope of protection' — these can be reconciled but the language tension is worth flagging at COI issuance.

findings.requirement_type: CGL Primary & Noncontributory — CG 20 01
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.C: ... shall be primary insurance as respects the COUNTY ... shall be excess of the CONTRACTOR's insurance and shall not contribute with it. Maricopa §8.2.4: Contractor's insurance shall be primary insurance as respects County, and any insurance or self-insurance maintained by County shall not contribute to it.
findings.policy_quote: CG 20 01 12 19 — Primary And Noncontributory – Other Insurance Condition (CGL Pg 59).
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO Primary & Noncontributory endorsement (CG 20 01 12 19) is on the CGL. Trigger conditions: (1) AI is a Named Insured under such other insurance, and (2) written contract requires P&NC. Both Sacramento and Maricopa contracts trigger the second condition. This satisfies P&NC requirement when an AI is listed.
findings.plain_english: Your security-guards GL has the right primary & noncontributory endorsement — the same form needs to also be on your real primary GL.
findings.recommendation: Confirm CG 20 01 (or equivalent) is also endorsed on the Citizens primary CGL. Verify same form is on the Auto policy when reviewed.

findings.requirement_type: CGL Waiver of Subrogation — Missing
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.8: The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees for any claims arising out of Contractor's work or service.
findings.policy_quote: [No CGL Waiver of Subrogation endorsement found in Schedule of Forms. checklist.waiver_of_subrogation = false. CG 24 04 (Waiver of Transfer of Rights of Recovery Against Others) is not listed among the endorsements.]
findings.policy_page: Schedule of Forms (Pg 8) and full endorsement listing
findings.gap_description: Maricopa explicitly requires Waiver of Subrogation on GL. Sacramento §VIII requires it on WC and is silent on GL but it is best practice. The CGL Schedule of Forms does not show CG 24 04 (Blanket Waiver of Transfer of Rights of Recovery Against Others) or any equivalent. The checklist confirms waiver_of_subrogation: false on this CGL. Failing to provide the WoS endorsement could allow the carrier to subrogate against the County after paying a claim — exposing Run-Test to indemnity / contract-breach claims from the County.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract specifically requires that your insurance company give up its right to come after the County after paying a claim. Your security-guards GL does not have this endorsement. If the carrier paid a county-related claim and then turned around to sue the County, the County would come right back at you for breach of contract. Adding the endorsement is usually free or nearly so.
findings.recommendation: Endorse blanket Waiver of Subrogation (CG 24 04 or equivalent) on the CGL. Confirm same on the Citizens primary CGL when produced. Confirm WoS endorsements on Auto, WC (state-specific WC waiver — AZ blanket and CA WC 04 03 06 if performing CA work), and any Inland Marine policy.
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever had your insurance carrier subrogate against one of your customers after a claim — and how did that customer react?
When your COIs are issued to the counties, does the certificate explicitly show a waiver of subrogation in the description box, or is it just generic?
If your carrier paid out on a Maricopa-related GL claim and then sued Maricopa to recover, how would your relationship with Maricopa survive that?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation (Maricopa 30-day Material Change Notice)
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. Contractor must provide to Maricopa County, within two business days of receipt, if they receive notice of a policy that has been or will be suspended, canceled, materially changed for any reason ...
findings.policy_quote: IL 02 58 04 21 (AZ Changes – Cancellation and Nonrenewal, Pg 14) — after 60 days in force: 10 days nonpayment / 45 days other reasons. No designated-entity NOC endorsement found that names Maricopa County and provides direct carrier-to-County notice.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.15 contemplates direct carrier-to-County 30-day cancellation/material-change notice. The standard ACORD COI cancellation language is no longer accepted in many counties. While Run-Test bears the contractual notice obligation (must relay within 2 business days), best practice is to also have a Designated Entity NOC endorsement (e.g., CG 20 12 / IL 12 01 / Hanover 401-1235 equivalent) naming Maricopa County so the carrier provides direct notice. The CGL has the AZ amendatory which gives 45 days for non-nonpayment cancellations after 60 days in force — this exceeds the 30-day requirement on duration but still places the notification burden on the insured. No specific designated-entity NOC was located. The broker target of 90 days is also not met.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants 30 days' notice if your insurance changes or is canceled. The contract puts that obligation on you, not on the carrier. There's no special endorsement on file naming Maricopa to get direct notice from the carrier. This is more of a process risk than a coverage risk — but if you accidentally miss relaying a cancellation notice, you're in material breach. As a broker, our target is 90 days of cancellation notice — your current policy gives 45.
findings.recommendation: Endorse a Designated Entity NOC for Maricopa (and Sacramento, listed customers) on every policy. Set up a process — in your broker's certificate management system — that automatically forwards any carrier cancellation, nonrenewal, or material-change notice to listed county counterparties within 2 business days. Long term, push for 90-day notice provisions at renewal.
discoveryQuestions: If your carrier sent a cancellation notice tomorrow because a premium check bounced, how confident are you that the right person at Run-Test would forward it to Maricopa within 2 business days?
Are you tracking which county counterparties need to receive direct cancellation notices — and do those names appear on your insurance policies?
Have you ever had a carrier nonrenew with short notice — and how did your customer relationships handle the gap?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Per-Project Aggregate (Sacramento §III.A)
findings.contract_quote: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503 Amendment-Aggregate Limits of Insurance (Per Project).
findings.policy_quote: [checklist.per_project_aggregate = false. No CG 25 03 or CG 25 04 endorsement located in Schedule of Forms.]
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §III.A requires Per-Project Aggregate (CG 25 03) IF Contractor is engaged in construction projects. Run-Test's core operations are election services — not construction — so the requirement may not be triggered. However, if Run-Test ever performs physical installation, equipment install, or any 'construction' style work for a county, this becomes mandatory. The CGL does not have CG 25 03/04. Same likely for the Citizens primary CGL until verified.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento wants you to have separate per-project aggregate limits — but only if you're doing construction work. As an election services manufacturer, you're probably not. But if a county ever asked you to install equipment on-site or do anything 'construction-like,' you'd need this endorsement. It's free or low-cost to add and protects your aggregate from being burned through by one bad project.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether Run-Test's scope of work for any county includes physical installation or construction. If yes, endorse CG 25 03 (Per Project Aggregate) on both the security-guards CGL and the Citizens primary CGL. If no, document the determination so the question doesn't recur at every COI issuance.
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test physically install any equipment at county sites, or is everything shipped to the county and they install it themselves?
If a county asked you to send a tech to install a ballot scanner on-site, would your standard process check whether the right insurance endorsements are in place first?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Unintentional Errors or Omissions Giveback
findings.contract_quote: [Broker best-practice — RMF General All Policies item 2.]
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1050 00 01 25 — Unintentional Errors or Omissions: 'Insured's failure to disclose hazards at inception not prejudicial unless intentional.'
findings.gap_description: CGL has dedicated Unintentional E&O endorsement (00 GL1050) protecting against innocent failure to disclose hazards at inception. Best practice — confirm the Citizens primary CGL has equivalent.
findings.plain_english: If your team accidentally forgot to tell the carrier about something at policy inception, the carrier can't deny coverage over it as long as it wasn't intentional. This is a small but meaningful protection — good to have.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the Citizens primary CGL has the equivalent giveback. Push for it on every line of the program at next renewal.

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Notice and Knowledge of Occurrence (Officer-Limited)
findings.contract_quote: [Broker best-practice — RMF General All Policies item 4 + CGL item 25.]
findings.policy_quote: [No 'Knowledge of Occurrence' / 'Notice Manager' / 'Imputation of Knowledge' endorsement located in CGL Schedule of Forms. Standard CG 00 01 04 13 (Pg 50, §IV.2) reads: 'You must see to it that we are notified as soon as practicable of an occurrence ...' — without an officer-limiting amendment, ANY employee's knowledge of an occurrence triggers the duty.]
findings.gap_description: Best practice is to endorse Knowledge of Occurrence so that only the Risk Manager / Officer / person responsible for insurance triggers the duty to report. With 50–200 employees, a low-level employee's awareness of an incident — never reported up — could later be used by the carrier to argue late notice and deny coverage. Not endorsed on this CGL.
findings.plain_english: If a warehouse worker sees a near-miss accident and doesn't tell anyone, the insurance company can later argue 'your company knew about this and didn't report it' and try to deny the claim. The fix is a small endorsement that says only your officer or risk manager's knowledge counts. It's easy to add — just nobody asked.
findings.recommendation: Endorse 'Knowledge of Occurrence' / 'Notice Manager' on every applicable policy in the program (GL, Auto, WC, Cyber, E&O). This is the single most-requested broker giveback for mid-size operations.
discoveryQuestions: If a forklift incident happened in your warehouse and the team handled it informally without telling management, do you know whether your insurance would still pay if a claim came in 18 months later?
Who at Run-Test is the designated 'risk officer' your broker has named to your carrier — and does every employee know to escalate incidents to that person?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Mental Anguish in Bodily Injury Definition
findings.contract_quote: [Broker best-practice — RMF CGL item 23.]
findings.policy_quote: Standard ISO CG 00 01 04 13 (Pg 53) Definition 4: '"Bodily injury" means bodily injury, sickness or disease sustained by a person, including death resulting from any of these at any time.' No mental-anguish-stand-alone endorsement located.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO CG 00 01 04 13 BI definition does NOT include mental anguish as a stand-alone covered injury — most courts require physical injury for mental anguish to be covered as part of BI. Best practice is to endorse the BI definition to include mental anguish in and of itself (not tied to physical injury). For a security operation involving force, restraint, or property protection, mental-anguish-only claims are realistic.
findings.plain_english: If someone claims emotional distress without any physical injury, your standard GL might not pay. There's an endorsement that adds 'mental anguish' as its own type of bodily injury — it's commonly available and worth asking for, especially since your security operations involve force-based interactions.
findings.recommendation: Request a Mental Anguish endorsement on both the security-guards CGL and the Citizens primary CGL at renewal. Confirm Auto policy has same.

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Care, Custody and Control
findings.contract_quote: [Broker best-practice — RMF CGL item 2.]
findings.policy_quote: Standard CG 00 01 04 13 (Pg 43) §I.A.2.j Damage to Property exclusions, including '(4) Personal property in the care, custody or control of the insured.' Coverage Extension 00 GL1051 (Pg 28) restores items (4)-(6) of the property exclusion ONLY for PD arising out of work/services listed on the Dec.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test handles county property — ballots, election technology, voter mail, county-supplied equipment — that could be in their care, custody, or control. Standard CCC exclusion would bar coverage. The Coverage Extension 00 GL1051 partially restores PD coverage for declared services BUT this monoline only declares security operations. The actual care/custody exposure is on the Citizens primary CGL — must verify CCC giveback there. Also relevant to Sacramento §IX (Inland Marine WoS) — voter mail and election equipment in transit may be covered under an Inland Marine policy.
findings.plain_english: When you take possession of a county's ballots, voter mail, or election equipment to process them, that's their property in your control. Your GL has a standard exclusion for that kind of damage. There's a partial fix on this policy but it only applies to security operations — your real exposure is on the Citizens GL. Plus, Inland Marine coverage is the real way to insure ballots and equipment in transit.
findings.recommendation: Verify CCC exposure on Citizens primary CGL — request a Care/Custody/Control giveback if not already in place. Determine whether Run-Test maintains an Inland Marine policy covering voter mail in transit, election equipment, and high-value computers (Sacramento §IX requires WoS endorsement on IM). If no IM policy, evaluate the gap given high-value equipment client profile.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Inland Marine policy (if in force) — not provided for audit

findings.requirement_type: Missing Inland Marine Policy — Equipment in Transit / High-Value Equipment
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR ... shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: [No Inland Marine policy in audit package.]
findings.gap_description: Run-Test profile flags 'high-value equipment' and operations include election mail in transit nationwide and ballot processing technology. Standard property forms typically exclude property in transit and off-premises. Inland Marine is the proper coverage for: (a) voter mail in transit, (b) ballot scanners and election technology equipment in transit/off-premises, (c) computer equipment, (d) accounts receivable / valuable papers (voter registration data printouts). Sacramento §IX makes WoS conditional on IM existing — if Run-Test maintains IM, the WoS endorsement must be in place. Cannot determine without IM policy.
findings.plain_english: You ship ballots, election mail, and high-value election technology around the country. A standard property policy doesn't usually cover stuff in transit. Inland Marine is the policy that does. We didn't see one in your file. If you don't have it, a truck accident, a theft of a ballot scanner shipment, or a fire on a printing press could be a six- or seven-figure uninsured loss.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether Inland Marine is in force. If yes, produce for audit and confirm blanket WoS endorsement is in place (Sacramento §IX). If no, evaluate exposure: catalog equipment values, in-transit shipments per year, off-premises equipment, voter data on portable media. Place IM coverage with adequate limits (often $1M–$10M depending on max single shipment value).

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Total Pollution Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: [RMF CGL item 31; cross-program pollution analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1047 00 01 25 — Total Pollution Exclusion with Hostile Fire and Self-Defense Spray Exception (Pg 21). Replaces ISO Exclusion f. Pollution. Exception only for hostile fire heat/smoke/fumes and use of mace/pepper spray normal to security operations. Hanover Umbrella 475-0027 (Pg 44) — Total Pollution Exclusion on Coverage A. Umbrella main form §VII.3.j — pollution excluded on Coverage B.
findings.gap_description: CGL has Total Pollution Exclusion with extremely narrow carve-outs (hostile fire + mace/pepper spray for security ops only). Umbrella has matching pollution exclusions on both Coverage A and Coverage B. Run-Test is a manufacturer (printing/inks) and operates a 2800 S 36th St Phoenix facility — printing inks, cleaning solvents, generator fuel, HVAC refrigerants are all potential pollutants. Indoor air quality / mold-adjacent claims also potentially excluded. With ZERO pollution coverage anywhere in the program, any release-related claim is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Both your GL and your umbrella exclude pollution claims. As a manufacturer with printing inks, solvents, generator fuel, and HVAC chemicals at your Phoenix facility, an environmental release — even something as routine as a transformer leak or cleaning-solvent spill — would not be covered. There is also no Contractors Pollution Liability or Premises Pollution Liability in the program. For a manufacturing operation this is a real gap.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate need for Premises Pollution Liability or Site Pollution Liability covering the Phoenix manufacturing/processing facility. At minimum, a $1M PPL policy with on-site cleanup, third-party BI/PD, and natural resource damages. If transportation of inks/chemicals is involved, consider Contractors Pollution Liability. PFAS exclusion (00 MLL0008) on the GL is also worth flagging given regulatory trends — many printing inks contain PFAS.
discoveryQuestions: Have you done an environmental site assessment at 2800 S 36th St — and do you know the historical use of the property?
Your printing inks and cleaning chemicals — has a vendor or compliance audit ever raised PFAS or VOC concerns?
If a chemical spill at your facility caused a third-party loss, do you know whether your insurance would respond at all?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Data Privacy Law Violation Exclusion (CG 00 69)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.A: ... no policy or coverages may include any self-insured retention amount or any limitation, restriction or exclusion which is in addition to coverage requirements stated herein, without the express written approval of the County Risk Manager.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 69 12 23 — Exclusion – Violation Of Law Addressing Data Privacy: 'This insurance does not apply to ... arising directly or indirectly out of any action or omission that violates ... Biometric Information Privacy Act ... California Consumer Privacy Act ... GDPR ... or any other federal, state, local or foreign laws and any rules or regulations promulgated thereunder.'
findings.gap_description: CG 00 69 is a hard-form exclusion barring all GL coverage for claims tied to data privacy law violations — explicitly named: BIPA, CCPA, GDPR. For an election services vendor processing voter PII for 90M+ registered voters across 31 states, every state has some flavor of privacy/election data law, and California (where Sacramento contract is) has CCPA. This is also a technical NON-CONFORMANCE with Sacramento §II.A 'no additional exclusions or limitations' unless waived by Risk Manager. Coverage must come exclusively from a standalone Cyber/Privacy policy. Combined with CG 21 06 (Access/Disclosure) and CG 40 35 (Cyber Incident), the GL provides ZERO defense for any privacy-related claim.
findings.plain_english: Your GL has an absolute exclusion that names California's CCPA, Illinois' BIPA, and the European GDPR. Sacramento's contract says you can't have additional exclusions without their Risk Manager's approval — so this exclusion technically puts you out of compliance unless waived. More importantly, election services involve voter data in every state you operate, and any state attorney general or class action plaintiff alleging a privacy law violation will get NO defense or indemnity from your GL. That's a job for a separate Cyber policy.
findings.recommendation: Disclose CG 00 69 (and CG 21 06, CG 40 35) to Sacramento Risk Manager and request acknowledgment / approval. Long term, ensure standalone Cyber covers BIPA / CCPA / GDPR / state election data privacy. Consider whether Citizens primary CGL has the same exclusion (likely yes given current market) and disclose accordingly.
discoveryQuestions: When you presented your COI to Sacramento, did anyone disclose to the Risk Manager that your GL has a CCPA exclusion?
If a class-action plaintiff alleges a CCPA violation tomorrow tied to your handling of California voter data, do you know which policy will defend you?
Have your election clients in Illinois ever asked about BIPA compliance for biometric voter authentication tools or signature verification?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Cyber Incident Exclusion (CG 40 35)
findings.contract_quote: [Cross-program cyber gap analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: CG 40 35 12 23 — Exclusion – Cyber Incident: '... arising out of a "cyber incident"' — defined to include unauthorized access, malicious code, denial of service. Includes notification, credit monitoring, forensic, PR, data restoration, and extortion expenses.
findings.gap_description: Absolute cyber exclusion on GL. Confirms zero cyber coverage anywhere on the GL — not even an island of coverage for resulting bodily injury (some forms preserve a BI carve-out — this one does not). All cyber response costs explicitly excluded.
findings.plain_english: Your GL absolutely excludes any kind of cyber loss — ransomware, hacking, denial-of-service, data breach response. Combined with the data privacy exclusion above, your GL is a hard wall against cyber claims. Standalone cyber is the only solution.
findings.recommendation: See finding-003 — place / confirm standalone Cyber policy at $5M minimum. Maricopa contract requires it explicitly.
discoveryQuestions: If a ransomware attack hit your ballot processing systems on the Friday before an election, do you know who pays the ransom — and who pays the lost-revenue claim from the county whose election was delayed?
Have you ever modeled the financial impact of a ransomware attack during election week — and is your cyber limit calibrated to that scenario?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Personal Data / Confidential Information Exclusion (CG 21 06)
findings.contract_quote: [Cross-program privacy gap analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: CG 21 06 12 23 — Exclusion – Access Or Disclosure Of Confidential Or Personal Material Or Information: '... arising out of any access to or disclosure of any person's or organization's confidential or personal information, including ... financial information, credit card information, health information, biometric information, or any other type of nonpublic information.' Includes notification, credit monitoring, forensic, PR, data restoration, and extortion expenses.
findings.gap_description: Triple-stack with CG 00 69 and CG 40 35 — all three exclusions reinforce that GL has zero privacy/data coverage. Voter PII handling is core to Run-Test's operations.
findings.plain_english: Just to make sure there's no daylight: your GL also has a separate exclusion specifically for any claim involving access to or disclosure of confidential information — financial, health, biometric, or 'any nonpublic information.' Voter rolls are nonpublic information. All paths to GL recovery for a data event are closed.
findings.recommendation: See finding-003 / finding-022. Standalone Cyber must respond to every form of privacy-related claim at adequate limits.
discoveryQuestions: How many records of voter PII does your operation touch on a peak election week — and do you know the per-record breach response cost?
Have you ever had your IT security tested by an outside red team, and do they have visibility into the systems that hold voter data?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Certified Acts of Terrorism Excluded (CG 21 73)
findings.contract_quote: [Broker best-practice — RMF CGL item 32.]
findings.policy_quote: CG 21 73 01 15 — Exclusion of Certified Acts of Terrorism: '... arising directly or indirectly out of a "certified act of terrorism" as defined under TRIA.'
findings.gap_description: Certified terrorism is excluded on the GL. The umbrella also has a Certified Acts of Terrorism exclusion (475-0433, Pg 64) that conflicts with the umbrella's own TRIA disclosure (Pg 6) showing terrorism premium charged and not rejected. Election infrastructure is a high-profile soft target. Without a buy-back or standalone TRIA policy, terrorism-driven BI/PD is uninsured anywhere in the program.
findings.plain_english: If a terrorist attack hits your ballot processing facility — and that's exactly the kind of high-profile civic target that gets attention — your GL excludes it and so does your umbrella. There's a separate small premium charged on the umbrella for TRIA but the umbrella endorsement excludes it anyway, which is contradictory. Election services are a known target. Worth getting a separate buy-back or a TRIA endorsement that actually works.
findings.recommendation: Buy back TRIA on both the CGL and Umbrella. Resolve the umbrella conflict between TRIA disclosure (premium charged) vs. CAT exclusion endorsement — get carrier confirmation in writing. Consider a standalone Active Assailant / Active Shooter policy given the political sensitivity of election infrastructure.
discoveryQuestions: Have you done a physical security assessment of your Phoenix facility, given the political sensitivity of election infrastructure?
Do you know whether your terrorism premium on the umbrella is actually buying you anything, given that the umbrella also has a terrorism exclusion endorsement?
If an active assailant event happened at your facility, do you know which policy would respond to bodily injury, business interruption, and the inevitable PR cost?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Manufacturing Exclusions (PFAS, Lead, Asbestos, Silica, Phthalates on Umbrella)
findings.contract_quote: [Cross-program manufacturing exposure analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: 00 MLL0008 PFAS Exclusion (Pg 3); 00 GL1061 Lead Exclusion (Pg 35); 00 GL1062 Asbestos Exclusion (Pg 36); CG 21 96 Silica Exclusion (Pg 67). Umbrella 475-0639 Phthalates (Pg 70); 475-0057 Lead (Pg 50); 475-0084 Silica (Pg 54); main form §VII.1.b Asbestos.
findings.gap_description: Stack of manufacturing-relevant chemical exclusions with no givebacks. Run-Test's profile is 'Manufacturing' with printing inks, presses, and chemical processing. PFAS (in printing inks), phthalates (in plasticizers/inks), heavy metals, silica from paper dust, and lead trace exposures are all real for a printing operation. No coverage anywhere in the program for these chemical classes.
findings.plain_english: Your insurance stack excludes a lot of chemical exposures that are realistic for a printing/manufacturing operation: PFAS (forever chemicals, often in inks), phthalates (in some plasticizers), lead (trace in some inks), asbestos, silica (paper dust). One regulatory or class-action claim under any of these — especially PFAS, which is the next big tort wave — would be entirely on your balance sheet.
findings.recommendation: Conduct a chemical inventory at the Phoenix facility. Evaluate whether any inks, plasticizers, or processing chemicals contain PFAS or phthalates. Consider standalone Pollution policy to fill these gaps if exposure is meaningful. Push back at next renewal to negotiate carve-backs for incidental amounts in finished products.
discoveryQuestions: Has your ink supplier provided written confirmation that none of their products contain PFAS or PFOA above regulatory thresholds?
When did you last conduct an industrial hygiene assessment of your printing operation?
Are any of the chemicals you use to clean printing equipment on the EPA or state-specific 'forever chemicals' radar?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — E&O Coverage D Shares Aggregate with A/B/C
findings.contract_quote: [Coverage form analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1049 — Errors & Omissions Coverage Extension (Coverage D): 'Subject to General Aggregate AND Each Occurrence limits — shared with A/B/C, NOT a separate aggregate.'
findings.gap_description: The CGL E&O extension shares limits with the GL coverages — meaning a single bad year of premises BI claims could exhaust the same aggregate that's also defending E&O claims. Adds limited value but does not substitute for standalone E&O. Numerous exclusions: intentional acts, statutory violations, contractual liability except insured contracts, fraud, intra-insured claims, employment law, electronic data damage. Damages exclude punitive and fines.
findings.plain_english: There's a small E&O extension built into your security GL but it eats from the same $3M annual cap as your regular GL claims. So if you have a bad GL year, your E&O is gone too. It's a small benefit, not a substitute for a real Professional Liability policy.
findings.recommendation: Treat 00 GL1049 as a small giveback for security operations only — not a substitute for the standalone Professional / Tech E&O policy required by Sacramento §II.D. See finding-004.
discoveryQuestions: If your security operation had a bad year and burned through the $3M GL aggregate, do you know that the small E&O extension would also be exhausted at the same time?
Have you considered that this E&O extension only covers your security operations, not your election services — which are your real exposure?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Canine Liability Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: [Coverage gap analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1048 00 01 25 — Canine Liability Exclusion: '... arising out of ownership, rental, maintenance or use of any dog or canine.'
findings.gap_description: Absolute K-9 exclusion. Significant for a security operation if K-9 units are deployed at the Phoenix facility, election warehouses, or in transit security. Coverage Endorsement 00 GL1063 Assault & Battery (Pg 37) is good news for force-based incidents but does NOT save canine-related claims.
findings.plain_english: If your security operation uses guard dogs anywhere — at your Phoenix facility, on customer election sites, or in transit — and one bites someone, your GL excludes it. If you do use K-9, this is a real gap.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether Run-Test's security operations use K-9 units. If yes, request a canine liability buy-back endorsement or place a separate canine liability rider. If no, document and move on.
discoveryQuestions: Does your security team use K-9 units at the Phoenix facility or any customer sites?
If you ever expanded into mobile security with K-9 capability, would the procurement process check the insurance implications first?

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Assault & Battery Coverage Extension
findings.contract_quote: [Coverage form analysis — security operations.]
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1063 00 01 25 — Assault and Battery Coverage Endorsement: 'Modifies Expected/Intended exclusion to NOT exclude (1) BI from use of physical force to protect persons or property; or (2) claims arising out of assault/battery by an employee.'
findings.gap_description: Critical for security guard operations — restores coverage that would otherwise be excluded under the standard ISO Expected/Intended exclusion. This is an above-market giveback for the security ops monoline.
findings.plain_english: Your security GL has the right A&B coverage extension — meaning if your security guards use force to protect persons or property, your insurance will respond. This is the right form for security operations.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Confirm equivalent on Citizens primary CGL if any security operations are also covered under that policy.

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Damage to Premises Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: [Broker best-practice — RMF CGL item 10.]
findings.policy_quote: Damage to Premises Rented to You: $1,000,000.
findings.gap_description: $1M Damage to Premises sublimit is at the high end of common offerings (vs. standard $50k–$300k). Above-market.
findings.plain_english: Your GL has $1M for damage to premises you rent — that's better than typical. If you're occupying a customer site temporarily and cause fire or water damage, you're well-covered up to $1M.
findings.recommendation: No action. Confirm Citizens primary CGL has equivalent.

findings.requirement_type: CGL — Duty to Defend
findings.contract_quote: [Broker best-practice — RMF CGL item 13.]
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §I.1.a — 'We will have the right and duty to defend the insured against any "suit" seeking those damages.'
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO duty-to-defend on GL. Carrier is required to defend. Meets best-practice.
findings.plain_english: Your GL gives the carrier the duty to defend you, not just the option. That's the standard you want — they have to provide a lawyer.
findings.recommendation: No action.

findings.requirement_type: CGL Cancellation Notice — 45 days vs Broker 90-day Target
findings.contract_quote: [Broker best-practice — RMF General item 1; Maricopa §8.2.15 30-day floor.]
findings.policy_quote: IL 02 58 04 21 (Pg 14): After 60 days in force: 10 days nonpayment / 45 days other reasons. Nonrenewal: 45 days advance notice.
findings.gap_description: AZ amendment provides 45 days for non-nonpayment cancellation. Meets Maricopa 30-day minimum. Misses the broker best-practice 90-day target. Same 45-day appears on Hanover Umbrella (475-0176, Pg 58).
findings.plain_english: Your policy gives you 45 days' notice if it's being canceled (other than for nonpayment). The minimum required by Maricopa is 30, so you meet that. But the broker target is 90 days — to give you time to find a replacement carrier without a coverage gap. We'd push for 90-day at renewal.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate 90-day cancellation notice at renewal. This is increasingly available at no/low cost for accounts of Run-Test's size.
discoveryQuestions: If your carrier nonrenewed your GL with 45 days' notice, do you know how long it would take your broker to remarket and place replacement coverage?
Has your broker ever pushed for 90-day notice on your renewals — and if not, are you willing to ask at the next renewal?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Professional Liability Excluded (Both Coverages)
findings.contract_quote: [Cross-program PL gap — Sacramento §II.E expressly forbids umbrella for PL anyway, but cross-program coverage analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: 475-0031 12 14 — Exclusion – Professional Liability (Coverage A): 'Excludes any liability arising out of rendering of or failure to render professional services, advice or instruction under Coverage A (Follow Form Excess).' Main form §VII.3.k — same on Coverage B.
findings.gap_description: Umbrella excludes Professional Liability on both Coverage A and Coverage B. Election technology / ballot processing / mail handling errors are pure 'professional services' — umbrella will NOT sit over a Professional Liability policy. Run-Test must rely on standalone PL/Tech E&O at adequate limits because the umbrella will not amplify them. Sacramento §II.E confirms umbrella cannot satisfy PL anyway, but the underlying exposure is much larger than $1M for a vendor handling 90M voters across 31 states.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella explicitly excludes professional services claims. So if you needed to stack the umbrella over your E&O policy to get higher limits, you can't. This is normal for umbrella policies but worth knowing — your real PL exposure is much larger than your $1M Sacramento minimum suggests, and you'd need a dedicated higher PL limit, not umbrella stacking.
findings.recommendation: Place standalone Professional / Tech E&O at the actual exposure level — likely $5M–$10M, not $1M. The $1M Sacramento minimum is a floor, not a recommendation. See finding-004.
discoveryQuestions: Has your broker ever explained that your umbrella will NOT extend over your professional liability — meaning your $10M umbrella is irrelevant to E&O claims?
Given the scale of your operations, what would a $25M election-day error claim do to your business if your E&O limit is only $1M and the umbrella doesn't apply?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Cyber/Privacy Exclusions on Both Coverages
findings.contract_quote: [Cross-program cyber gap analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: 475-0654 12 23 — Exclusion – Access or Disclosure of Confidential or Personal Material or Information and Electronic Data (Pg 72). 475-0655 12 23 — Exclusion – Violation of Law Addressing Data Privacy including BIPA, CCPA, GDPR (Pg 74). 475-0661 01 25 — Exclusion – Cyber Incident – Cyber Content (Pg 76).
findings.gap_description: Umbrella has triple-stack cyber/privacy exclusion on BOTH Coverage A (follow-form excess) and Coverage B (umbrella) — barring excess for data breach, privacy law violations, cyber incidents, and cyber-content torts (IP, plagiarism, defamation via electronic content). Critical for an election services vendor: any cyber incident maxing out the standalone cyber limit will NOT have umbrella drop-down. Maricopa requires $5M cyber per occurrence — must be entirely on the standalone cyber, no umbrella safety net.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella excludes everything cyber — data breaches, privacy law violations, ransomware, cyber-related defamation. So whatever your standalone cyber policy limit is, that's your absolute ceiling. If a voter PII breach exceeds your cyber limit, the umbrella will not pick up the rest. Given that election infrastructure breaches can run into the hundreds of millions when you factor in regulatory fines, notification of millions of records, and litigation, your standalone cyber limit needs to be calibrated to the actual exposure — not just to the $5M Maricopa minimum.
findings.recommendation: Size standalone Cyber to the underlying exposure, not the contract minimum. For an election vendor with 90M voters of data, $5M is likely far too low. Consider $10M–$25M cyber tower with multiple carriers if needed.
discoveryQuestions: If your cyber policy limit is $5M and you have a breach affecting 1M voter records, what's the per-record cost of breach response — and does that math suggest $5M is anywhere near enough?
Have you considered that your $10M umbrella provides ZERO drop-down for cyber, meaning cyber is the one line where your tower stops at the cyber primary limit?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Discrimination Exclusion (No Excess EPLI)
findings.contract_quote: [Cross-program EPLI excess analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: 475-0215 12 14 — Exclusion – Discrimination (Coverage A and B): 'Excludes liability arising from discrimination/humiliation based on age, gender, sexual orientation, marital status, race, nationality, religion, disability, or any violation of anti-discrimination laws.'
findings.gap_description: Umbrella will not sit over EPLI even if EPLI is in force — typical for follow-form excess. Multi-state employee count (50–200, 31 states including CA) means underlying EPLI limit is the ceiling. With CA exposure, $1M EPLI may be inadequate.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella excludes discrimination claims, which is normal — but it means whatever EPLI you have (or buy), that's your hard cap on employment-related claims. With operations in California and 50–200 employees, $1M EPLI is the floor, not the right answer.
findings.recommendation: If/when EPLI is placed (see finding-009), size to actual exposure — at minimum $2M, more likely $5M for multi-state including CA.
discoveryQuestions: Has your HR team modeled what a class-action wage-and-hour case in California could cost — and how that compares to a $1M or $2M EPLI limit?
Does your EPLI's defense-inside-or-outside-limits decision change your real protection against a multi-plaintiff class action?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — TRIA Premium Charged but Certified Acts Excluded (Internal Conflict)
findings.contract_quote: [Internal policy conflict analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: 401-1374 12 20 (Pg 6) — TRIA Disclosure: 'Total Terrorism Premium $75. Insured did NOT reject.' BUT 475-0433 01 15 (Pg 64) — 'Exclusion – Certified Acts of Terrorism: Excludes injury or damage arising directly or indirectly out of a certified act of terrorism on both Coverages A and B.'
findings.gap_description: TRIA Disclosure states $75 terrorism premium charged and that insured did NOT reject TRIA — typically that means TRIA is in force. But endorsement 475-0433 absolutely excludes Certified Acts of Terrorism on both coverages. These two read together create a contradiction. Possible interpretations: (a) the $75 was charged but coverage was rejected via the exclusion endorsement (carrier billing error), (b) the disclosure was an artifact and TRIA is actually excluded as documented in 475-0433, (c) the exclusion overrides the disclosure but the carrier owes a premium refund. Cannot resolve without carrier confirmation.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella has a contradiction. The disclosure says you paid $75 for terrorism coverage and didn't reject it. A separate endorsement says terrorism is excluded. Either way, you're not getting what you paid for — either the carrier owes you a $75 refund and there's no terrorism coverage, or there's terrorism coverage and the exclusion endorsement was added in error. Get clarity in writing before you need to find out at claim time.
findings.recommendation: Email Hanover requesting written clarification on whether terrorism coverage applies to the umbrella, and if so, on what terms. Get the answer in writing on carrier letterhead.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Pollution Excluded Both Coverages
findings.contract_quote: [Cross-program pollution analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: 475-0027 12 14 (Pg 44) — Total Pollution Exclusion on Coverage A. Main form §VII.3.j (Pg 35) — pollution excluded on Coverage B.
findings.gap_description: Pollution excluded everywhere — confirming finding-021 has no umbrella excess. Pollution claims are entirely uninsured.
findings.plain_english: The umbrella also excludes pollution — confirming the gap. Pollution claims have no insurance backstop anywhere in your program.
findings.recommendation: See finding-021 — place CPL or PPL.
discoveryQuestions: Has anyone walked you through what a five-figure cleanup of a printing-ink spill turns into when there's groundwater involvement and the EPA gets called?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Multiple Named Insured Endorsement (475-0174)
findings.contract_quote: [RMF General item 3.]
findings.policy_quote: 475-0174 12 14 — Multiple Named Insured Endorsement: Adds Runbeck Properties LLC, Runbeck Investments LLC, Runbeck Graphics Inc as Named Insureds.
findings.gap_description: Affiliates explicitly scheduled — reliable inclusion, no LLC carve-out. This is the right form (vs. a Broad Form Named Insured that might exclude LLCs).
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella explicitly names your real-estate LLC, your investment LLC, and your graphics company as covered. That's the right setup — better than relying on a broad-form endorsement that might leave LLCs out.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the same affiliates are scheduled (or properly extended) on every other policy in the program — GL, Auto, WC, Cyber, E&O, Crime, EPLI, D&O. Asymmetry across the program is the most common gap. See also finding-010 on the Inc/LLC mismatch on the parent operating entity.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Underlying Sublimits Exclusion (475-0613)
findings.contract_quote: [Coverage form analysis.]
findings.policy_quote: 475-0613 11 20 — Underlying Insurance Defined: 'sublimits or separate limits within an underlying policy that are not separately listed on the SCHEDULE OF UNDERLYING POLICIES are NOT considered underlying insurance — meaning the umbrella will NOT drop down/follow over those sublimited coverages.'
findings.gap_description: Critical structural limitation: any sublimit in an underlying policy (e.g., the GL Limited Theft Extension at $100k/$300k, the Lost Key Coverage sublimits, the various coverage extensions) is NOT amplified by the umbrella unless explicitly scheduled. Many sublimited coverages in the security-guards CGL (theft extension, lost keys, incidental medical malpractice) are stuck at primary sublimits with no excess available.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella only sits over the main limits of your underlying policies — not the various sublimited coverages within them. So if your GL has a $100k theft sublimit, your umbrella does NOT amplify that. Anything sublimited is capped at the sublimit and the umbrella won't help.
findings.recommendation: Audit every sublimit on every underlying policy. For sublimits that materially undersize the underlying exposure, either negotiate higher sublimits at next renewal or schedule them in the umbrella to allow drop-down. Sometimes the simpler path is a standalone policy for the line (e.g., move theft to a Crime policy with $1M limit).
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever pulled a list of every sublimit on every policy and asked your broker which ones the umbrella will and won't amplify?
Are there sublimited coverages — like theft, lost keys, incidental services — where your real exposure is bigger than the sublimit?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Defense Outside Limits / Right and Duty
findings.contract_quote: [Broker best-practice — RMF Umbrella items 5 and 11.]
findings.policy_quote: 475-0001 12 22 main policy form (Pg 24-37). Standard Hanover umbrella — Defense costs are outside the limit. Coverage A follows form. Coverage B has standard right-and-duty when underlying is exhausted.
findings.gap_description: Standard-market Hanover umbrella with defense-outside-limits and standard duty-to-defend when underlying exhausted. This is the correct setup.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella's defense costs are outside the limit (good — defense doesn't eat your $10M), and the carrier has the duty to defend if your underlying limits run out. Both correct.
findings.recommendation: No action.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Maintenance of Underlying
findings.contract_quote: [Broker best-practice — RMF Umbrella item 6.]
findings.policy_quote: 475-0001 §VIII conditions (Pg 36) — Maintenance of Underlying Insurance.
findings.gap_description: Standard maintenance-of-underlying language. Insured must keep underlying in force; if underlying is reduced/exhausted by claims, umbrella drops down at the underlying limits. If insured allows underlying to lapse, umbrella applies as if underlying remained in force at scheduled limits — i.e., insured eats the difference.
